chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Unlisted Market — What It Is and How It Works

lessons.title: What Are Pre-IPO and Unlisted Shares

children.text: On a Tuesday evening, Meena gets a WhatsApp forward from a stockbroker she has never met. The message says he can get her "pre-IPO shares of Vayu Mobility, India's hottest EV unicorn, at just ₹450 a share, guaranteed listing gains." Meena has ₹15 lakh sitting idle and has heard enough stories about early investors in companies like Zomato and Nykaa turning small stakes into life-changing money before those companies listed. Before she replies with her PAN and a screenshot of a bank transfer, she needs to understand exactly what she would be buying, because "pre-IPO shares" is not one thing. It is a label, and labels can be wrong.

body.text: An unlisted share is not a worse share. It is the exact same ownership stake in a company as a listed share, minus a functioning, regulated market where you can sell it the moment you want to.

children.text: What "Unlisted" Actually Means

markDefs.definition: The government authority under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) that registers companies and maintains their statutory filings.
Held electronically in a demat account rather than as a physical share certificate. SEBI requires unlisted public companies to issue and transfer shares only in dematerialised form.

children.text: Every company incorporated in India, private or public, issues shares to its owners the moment it is set up. That is true whether it is a five-person startup or a listed giant. What makes a share listed is a separate, later step: the company applies to a recognised stock exchange, meets that exchange's disclosure and financial thresholds, and its shares are admitted to trading there. A share stays unlisted for as long as that step has not happened, whether the company is six months old, sixty years old, or has no intention of ever listing. Every share, listed or not, still has to be registered with the
Registrar of Companies (RoC)
and, if it is to be freely transferable, held in
dematerialised
form in a demat account.

body.label: Most Indian companies never list
body.context: Around 2,000 to 2,500 companies trade on the NSE and BSE combined, against well over 16 lakh active companies registered with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.

children.text: Two Different Ideas People Mix Up: "Unlisted Shares" and "Pre-IPO Shares"

markDefs.definition: The detailed disclosure document a company must file with SEBI before an IPO, covering its financials, business risks and how the IPO proceeds will be used. It becomes public on SEBI's website once filed.

children.text: Every pre-IPO share is unlisted, but most unlisted shares are nowhere near an IPO. "Unlisted" is the broad, technical category: any share not admitted to trading on a stock exchange. "Pre-IPO" is a much narrower claim: that the company is actually on a credible path to listing, usually within the next one to three years. A hundred-year-old family-run manufacturer with no plans to ever raise public capital is unlisted. A startup that has just filed its
Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP)

with SEBI is both unlisted and genuinely pre-IPO. The broker pitching Meena used the word "pre-IPO" because it sounds more exciting and more time-sensitive than "unlisted." That does not make it accurate.

body.title: Unlisted vs Pre-IPO: Same Umbrella, Different Claims

columns.label: Unlisted shares (the broad category)
points: Any share not trading on the NSE or BSE, for any reason
May belong to a company with no listing plans at all, ever
Includes decades-old family businesses, wholly owned subsidiaries, and closely-held companies
Example: Kannan Devan Hills Plantations, a large tea estate company whose shares have changed hands among a closed group of holders for decades, with no IPO in sight

columns.label: Pre-IPO shares (a narrower subset)
points: Unlisted, plus a credible, near-term path to listing
Usually backed by a filed DRHP, an announced listing timeline, or strong, reported market expectation
Carries real but different risks: listing can be delayed, priced lower than hoped, or shelved entirely
Example: Tata Capital and HDB Financial Services both traded actively in the unlisted market for years before their shares were eventually listed through an IPO

body.text: A useful filter: if a seller calls something "pre-IPO" but cannot point you to a DRHP filed with SEBI, an announced listing timeline, or at least credible news coverage of IPO plans, treat the word as marketing, not information. What you are actually being offered is simply an unlisted share, priced as if a listing were imminent.

children.text: Where These Shares Actually Come From
Unlisted shares in circulation in India come from a handful of real sources, and knowing which one you are looking at tells you a lot about the risk.

body.caption: The main sources of unlisted shares an Indian investor might be offered

cells: Employee ESOPs
Employees at startups are granted stock options that vest over years. Long before any IPO, some choose to sell part of their vested shares for liquidity, often through a dealer or platform.
Early employees at companies like Flipkart and Ola sold vested ESOP shares years before any listing event.
Early investor secondaries
Angel investors or early VCs sell part of their stake to a new buyer without waiting for the company's own exit event.
A seed-round angel selling part of their holding to a later-stage fund or HNI buyer.
Private placement allotments
A company raises a fresh round and issues new shares directly to investors under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, with no exchange involved.
A Series B investor receiving freshly issued CCPS directly from the company.
Old-economy family and closely-held companies
Companies that were never built as VC-funded startups and have no listing plans, but still have shareholders who occasionally trade shares privately.
Kannan Devan Hills Plantations and similar long-standing unlisted businesses.

children.text: Notice what none of these sources involve: an exchange, a public order book, or a continuously updated market price. That absence is the single biggest thing that changes when a share is unlisted, and it is worth sitting with before the next lesson, which covers how these shares are actually bought and sold in practice.
Same Ownership, a Very Different Experience

markDefs.definition: SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements, 2015 — the rules that force listed companies to regularly disclose financial results, shareholding patterns and material events to the public.

children.text: A listed share and an unlisted share of two similar companies can represent an identical percentage of ownership, an identical claim on profits, and an identical vote at a shareholder meeting. What differs is everything around that ownership. A listed company must comply with SEBI's
Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR)

, publishing quarterly results, shareholding patterns and material announcements that anyone can read for free. An unlisted company, even a large and well-known one, has no such obligation to the public. You cannot pull up its quarterly numbers on screener.in the way you can for a listed company, because there usually is nothing there to pull up.

body.caption: What actually changes when a share is listed vs unlisted

cells: Selling it
Sell in seconds on an app like Zerodha, at a price the whole market can see
Find a buyer yourself or through a dealer; no guarantee one exists when you need it
Price discovery
Continuous, public, driven by lakhs of buyers and sellers
Negotiated deal by deal; dealer-quoted prices can vary widely and are not independently verified
Disclosure
Quarterly results, shareholding pattern and material events public under SEBI LODR
No public disclosure requirement; investors rely on whatever the company or seller chooses to share
Transferring shares
Instant, electronic, exchange-settled
Often needs the company's board approval and may be restricted by a Right of First Refusal in the company's Articles

markDefs.definition: A contractual right, usually written into a company's Articles of Association or Shareholders' Agreement, letting existing shareholders or the company match any outside offer and buy the shares first, before a new buyer is allowed in.

children.text: That last row matters more than it looks. Many private companies' Articles of Association give existing shareholders a
Right of First Refusal (RoFR)

, which means the company or its existing shareholders can insist on buying the shares first, at the same price, before an outside buyer is allowed in. A seller offering you unlisted shares should be able to show you that this step has been cleared, or you may end up with a signed deal that the company itself is entitled to block.

children.text: Back to Meena's WhatsApp Offer

body.title: Is This Actually Pre-IPO?
body.scenario: The broker tells Meena that Vayu Mobility will "list within 6 months, guaranteed" and that the ₹450 price is "already 40% below where it will list." He cannot show her a DRHP, only a one-page "fact sheet" with the company's logo and some growth numbers he says come from "internal sources."
body.prompt: Using what you now know about the difference between "unlisted" and "pre-IPO", what should Meena actually check before deciding, and what does the absence of a DRHP tell her?
body.modelAnswer: The absence of a filed DRHP is the single biggest red flag here. SEBI's website publicly lists every DRHP filed by a company planning an IPO, and checking it is free. If Vayu Mobility genuinely had a listing six months away, that filing would already be public, since the DRHP-to-listing process itself typically takes several months once filed. No DRHP means "pre-IPO" is, at best, the broker's guess and, at worst, a sales pitch to move an illiquid unlisted share at an inflated price. Meena should also ask for the company's cap table or at least a shareholder record to confirm the shares are genuinely allotted and would be transferred into her name, verify the broker's identity and any SEBI registration, and independently find at least one other source quoting a similar price for the same shares before treating ₹450 as a real market price rather than a number the broker chose.

body.title: Before You Call Anything "Pre-IPO", Check These
steps: Has the company actually filed a DRHP with SEBI? Check sebi.gov.in directly, not the seller's word for it.
Is there a specific, publicly reported listing timeline, or only the seller's verbal promise?
Can the seller show you a cap table extract or shareholder record proving the shares exist and are theirs to sell?
Is the quoted price close to what other independent sources report for the same company's shares, or is it an outlier?
Is the seller or platform identifiable and traceable, not just a phone number on WhatsApp?

body.title: Unlisted vs Pre-IPO
body.question: A 70-year-old private manufacturing company has never raised venture capital, has no plans to go public, but occasionally sees its shares change hands privately among a small group of shareholders. How should this company's shares be described?
options: Unlisted shares, but not pre-IPO shares
body.explanation: Every share not admitted to trading on a stock exchange is unlisted, but "pre-IPO" specifically implies a credible, near-term path to listing. A company with no IPO plans at all is unlisted without being pre-IPO, no matter how long its shares have quietly changed hands privately.

body.title: The Core Distinction
body.textWithBlank: Every pre-IPO share is unlisted, but not every unlisted share is ___.
body.explanation: Pre-IPO is a narrower claim than unlisted. It requires an actual, credible path to listing, not just the absence of one.

body.label: SEBI: Check filed DRHPs
body.description: Search SEBI's public filings to check whether a company claiming to be "pre-IPO" has actually filed a Draft Red Herring Prospectus, before trusting a seller's timeline.

body.title: How to actually verify a company exists and is active

children.text: Every company incorporated in India, listed or not, has a Corporate Identification Number (CIN) and a public filing history on the MCA portal.
Go to mca.gov.in and use the "View Company/LLP Master Data" service.
Search by company name to get its CIN, registration date, and current status (Active, Strike Off, Under Liquidation, and so on).
A company showing as "Strike Off" or "Under Liquidation" cannot legitimately be selling you fresh shares, whatever a broker claims.
This single check takes under two minutes and costs nothing, yet catches a meaningful share of the offers that turn out to be fabricated or stale.

cards.definition: Any share not admitted to trading on a recognised stock exchange like the NSE or BSE, regardless of the company's size, age or future listing plans.
An unlisted share in a company with a credible, near-term path to listing, typically backed by a filed DRHP or a publicly reported IPO timeline.
The detailed disclosure document filed with SEBI before an IPO, covering financials, risks and use of proceeds. Publicly available once filed.
A contractual right letting existing shareholders or the company match an outside offer and buy shares first, before a new buyer is allowed in.
Held electronically in a demat account rather than as a physical certificate.
SEBI's rules requiring listed companies to regularly disclose financial results and material events to the public.
A unique number assigned to every company registered in India, searchable on the MCA portal to verify a company's active status.

points: Every company issues shares at incorporation. "Listed" is a separate, later status that requires meeting a stock exchange's own admission criteria.
"Unlisted" is the broad category: any share not on an exchange. "Pre-IPO" is a narrower claim requiring a credible, near-term path to listing, usually a filed DRHP.
The overwhelming majority of Indian companies are unlisted and always will be. Being unlisted says nothing by itself about whether a company is good, bad, or about to list.
Unlisted shares typically come from ESOP sales, early investor secondaries, private placements, or long-standing closely-held companies. The source tells you a lot about the risk.
What changes with listing status is liquidity, price discovery, public disclosure, and how easily shares can be transferred, not the underlying ownership itself.
Before trusting the label "pre-IPO", check SEBI's public filings for a DRHP and verify the company's active status on the MCA portal. Both checks are free and take minutes.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Meena and Vayu Mobility are fictional and used purely for illustration. Unlisted and pre-IPO shares are high-risk, illiquid investments that can be difficult or impossible to sell when you want to, and their pricing is not independently verified the way listed share prices are. Always verify claims independently, such as through SEBI's and the MCA's public filings, before acting on any unlisted-share offer.
